triage.name: Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder
triage.reason: Common childhood behavioral presentation with inattention, impulsivity and hyperactivity; diagnosis reachable through structured history from parent and child, with school and developmental context.

demographics: Boys are diagnosed about twice as often as girls, largely because hyperactive-impulsive symptoms bring boys to attention earlier
Girls are more likely to have the inattentive presentation and to be diagnosed later, often in adolescence or adulthood
Symptoms must be present before age 12 for the diagnosis, though the evaluation may happen much later
A substantial minority of adults first seek care in adulthood after a child is diagnosed

risk_factors.text: Very low birth weight or prematurity
Early severe psychosocial deprivation or institutional care

family_history: ADHD in a parent or sibling
Learning problems or repeated grades in a parent
Anxiety or mood disorder in a parent
social_history: Academic underperformance or repeated discipline at school
Frequent job changes or lost jobs in adults

chief_complaints.text: My teacher says I can't sit still and I keep getting in trouble for talking
I can't focus on my schoolwork, I lose everything and my grades are slipping
My mind jumps from one thing to another and I never finish anything
I feel restless all the time and I interrupt people without meaning to

hpi.onset: Symptoms have been present since early childhood, usually before age 6, though parents often only recognize them as a problem once school demands increase
hpi.duration: Chronic, present for at least 6 months and typically years
hpi.progression: Persistent rather than episodic; hyperactivity often becomes less visible with age while inattention, disorganization and impulsivity continue into adolescence and adulthood
hpi.quality: A lifelong pattern of inattention, impulsivity and, in many, hyperactivity that is present across more than one setting such as home and school or work
hpi.severity: Mild to severe; severity is judged by how much it impairs school, work, friendships or family life
hpi.timing: Daily and continuous rather than episodic; worse during tasks that require sustained mental effort, quiet sitting or waiting
aggravating: Sitting still in class or meetings

associated_symptoms.text: Careless mistakes and missed details in schoolwork or work
Trouble sustaining attention on tasks or play
Easily distracted by outside noise or their own thoughts
Losing everyday items like pencils, keys, phone or homework
Fidgeting, tapping hands or feet, or squirming in the seat
Interrupting others or blurting out answers
Leaving the seat when expected to stay seated
Feeling internally restless in teens and adults even without visible movement
Poor sleep, hard to settle at night

pertinent_negatives: Symptoms began only after a stressful event or a recent loss
Symptoms are limited to one setting only
Periods of elevated mood with decreased need for sleep
Episodes of staring spells with loss of awareness
New focal weakness, numbness or gait change
Symptoms started abruptly in an older adult

positives.text: Low mood or worry about school performance

argues_against: Staring spells with loss of awareness

positives.text: Feeling tired during the day from poor sleep

argues_against: Constitutional symptoms suggesting another systemic illness
Thyroid disease presenting with restlessness and poor concentration
Gastrointestinal illness causing poor school attendance

atypical.how_it_differs: Preschool-aged children present mainly with hyperactivity, impulsivity and tantrums rather than clear inattention, and the history comes almost entirely from parents and daycare staff.

Adults often present with disorganization, forgetfulness and job or relationship problems rather than visible hyperactivity, and symptoms may be mistaken for normal aging or mild cognitive impairment.
Women may first seek care when pregnancy or a new baby makes organization and attention problems harder to manage, and treatment decisions must weigh fetal and breastfeeding safety.

general.mild: Alert, engaged, able to sit through most of the visit with occasional prompting
general.moderate: Restless, frequently out of the seat or touching objects in the room, needs repeated redirection to finish the visit
general.severe: Constantly moving, interrupts the interview, cannot stay seated long enough to complete the exam without a parent or staff member redirecting
general.critical: Marked agitation or unsafe impulsivity requiring immediate behavioral management

findings.maneuver: Measure height, weight and vital signs and plot them on a growth chart
findings.finding: Normal growth parameters and vital signs

findings.maneuver: Observe the patient while seated during the interview
findings.finding: Fidgeting, tapping hands or feet, squirming in the chair

findings.maneuver: Observe whether the patient stays seated when expected
findings.finding: Leaves the seat or climbs on furniture during the visit
Blurts out answers, interrupts the examiner or parent

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to repeat a short series of digits or to follow a multi-step instruction
findings.finding: Loses track of the task, needs the instruction repeated

findings.maneuver: Assess orientation, alertness and general cognitive screen
findings.finding: Alert, oriented, no confusion or clouding of consciousness

findings.maneuver: Perform a focused neurologic exam including cranial nerves, strength, coordination and gait
findings.finding: No focal deficit, normal coordination and gait

findings.maneuver: Screen hearing and vision (or review recent screening results)
Inspect the skin for bruising or injuries

initial.why: Screens for anemia or another blood disorder that can cause poor attention and fatigue
initial.only_if: pallor, fatigue or a bleeding history suggests anemia

initial.why: Thyroid disease can mimic restlessness and poor concentration
initial.only_if: restlessness, poor concentration, heat or cold intolerance, or poor growth

initial.why: Iron deficiency can cause inattention and fatigue
Deficiency can cause cognitive and attention complaints
Lead exposure is a risk factor and can cause inattention and hyperactivity
initial.only_if: known exposure, pica, or an at-risk home environment

supporting.why: Uncontrolled diabetes can cause fatigue and poor concentration
Cushing syndrome can present with poor concentration and mood change
supporting.only_if: growth failure, weight gain or striae

supporting.why: Inflammatory or autoimmune illness can cause fatigue and school problems
supporting.only_if: systemic symptoms such as fever, rash or joint pain

not_indicated.why: Not routine in a well-appearing child with classic ADHD symptoms
No role in the evaluation of ADHD
Liver enzymes are not part of the diagnostic workup
Not routine when there are no thyroid symptoms
Not routine without signs of iron deficiency
Not routine without risk factors or neurologic findings
Only for children with known exposure or risk factors
Not routine without diabetes symptoms or risk factors
Not routine without features of cortisol excess
Not part of the ADHD workup
Not part of the ADHD workup
Not part of the ADHD workup
Not indicated unless there are staring spells or suspected seizures
Not indicated for ADHD; reserved for focal neurologic findings or suspected structural cause

decision_points: Diagnosis is clinical: symptoms before age 12, present in more than one setting, causing impairment, and not better explained by another condition
Gather information from parents and teachers using standardized rating scales; a child's self-report alone is not enough
Screen for comorbid anxiety, depression, learning disorders, sleep problems and substance use
Order labs only to exclude mimics suggested by history or exam, not as a routine panel
Before starting stimulant medication, check blood pressure, heart rate and growth; obtain an ECG only if there is known cardiac disease, syncope, or a concerning family history of sudden death

criteria.name: ADHD symptom pattern
criteria.summary: A persistent pattern of inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity that interferes with functioning or development, with several symptoms present before age 12, present in two or more settings, and clearly interfering with school, work or social life. Symptoms are not better explained by another mental disorder.
items: Several inattentive or hyperactive-impulsive symptoms present before age 12
Symptoms present in two or more settings (home, school, work, with friends)
Symptoms interfere with or reduce the quality of social, academic or occupational functioning
Symptoms are not solely part of another disorder such as anxiety, depression or a psychotic disorder

criteria.name: Presentation types
criteria.summary: The presentation is described by which symptom group predominates over the past 6 months.

differential.name: Anxiety disorder
differential.why_considered: Restlessness, poor concentration, irritability and trouble settling are shared with ADHD, and the two often occur together
differential.trigger: Symptoms that are clearly worse in one setting, or that began after a stressor or a period of worry

history: Worry is the core problem, not just distractibility
Symptoms are worse before tests, performances or social events
Physical symptoms of anxiety such as stomachaches or headaches before school
Symptoms may be present only in some settings rather than across home and school
exam: Looks tense or worried during the visit
Can usually sit and complete tasks when calm
No pervasive pattern of impulsive interruption
labs: No lab test confirms anxiety; thyroid studies only if thyroid symptoms

differential.name: Major depressive disorder
differential.why_considered: Poor concentration, low motivation, forgetfulness and school decline overlap with ADHD, especially in adolescents
differential.trigger: A change from a previous level of functioning, with sadness, loss of interest or sleep and appetite change

history: Symptoms started or clearly worsened after a change in mood
Sadness, hopelessness or loss of interest most days
Sleep and appetite change
Symptoms are episodic rather than lifelong
labs: No lab test confirms depression; screen for thyroid disease only if suggested

differential.name: Sleep disorder or chronic sleep deprivation
differential.why_considered: Daytime inattention, irritability and hyperactivity can all result from poor or insufficient sleep
differential.trigger: Snoring, witnessed pauses in breathing, restless sleep, or a schedule that leaves too little time in bed

history: Loud snoring or witnessed apneas
Wakes unrefreshed despite adequate time in bed
Daytime sleepiness rather than only restlessness
Symptoms improve when sleep is treated or extended
exam: Enlarged tonsils, crowded oropharynx, or obesity
labs: No routine labs; consider thyroid studies if growth or weight concerns
imaging: Not routinely indicated; sleep study is the key test

differential.name: Specific learning disorder
differential.why_considered: A child who cannot keep up with reading or math may look inattentive, avoidant and frustrated in class
differential.trigger: Academic difficulty that is out of proportion to attention, or that persists in one subject only

history: Trouble is concentrated in one academic area such as reading or math
Attention is normal during non-academic or hands-on activities
Often a family history of reading or spelling problems
exam: Normal attention and behavior outside academic tasks

differential.name: Autism spectrum disorder
differential.why_considered: Social difficulty, repetitive behavior, intense narrow interests and trouble with transitions can be mistaken for ADHD
differential.trigger: Early social-communication differences or repetitive or restricted behaviors

history: Delayed or atypical language and social milestones
Poor eye contact and difficulty reading social cues
Repetitive movements or insistence on sameness
Symptoms present from the first years of life, not just when school demands increase
labs: Genetic testing may be offered when dysmorphic features or developmental delay are present

differential.name: Absence seizures
differential.why_considered: Brief staring spells with loss of awareness can be mistaken for daydreaming and inattention
differential.trigger: Staring spells that interrupt activity, with no response during the spell and no memory of it afterward

history: Sudden brief staring spells lasting seconds, many times a day
Activity stops and resumes abruptly
No memory of the episode
May have eyelid fluttering or lip smacking
exam: May be provoked by hyperventilation in the office
imaging: MRI brain only if focal features or abnormal EEG localization

differential.name: Thyroid disease
differential.why_considered: Restlessness, fidgeting, poor concentration and irritability can be caused by an overactive thyroid
differential.trigger: Weight loss, heat intolerance, tremor, palpitations or poor growth despite good appetite

history: Weight loss despite increased appetite
Heat intolerance and sweating
Palpitations
Symptoms are new rather than lifelong
labs: Abnormal TSH with elevated free T4
imaging: Thyroid ultrasound or uptake scan only if a nodule or goiter is found

differential.name: Substance use
differential.why_considered: Stimulant or cannabis use can cause restlessness, poor focus, declining school or work performance and irritability
differential.trigger: A change from a stable baseline, new social circle, or physical signs of use

history: Symptoms began or worsened after starting a substance
Use of stimulants, cannabis, alcohol or opioids
Decline in function that tracks with use
Drug-seeking behavior or withdrawal symptoms
labs: Urine drug screen positive for the substance

severity.mild: Symptoms are present but cause only minor difficulty; grades, friendships and family life are largely intact and the patient needs only monitoring, classroom accommodations or behavioral strategies
severity.moderate: Symptoms clearly interfere with school, work or relationships; the patient needs a structured behavioral plan and usually medication, with regular follow-up
severity.severe: Marked impairment across settings with failing grades, repeated discipline, lost jobs or strained relationships; needs combined behavioral and medication treatment with close follow-up and school or workplace support
severity.critical: Severe impulsivity or agitation that puts the patient or others in immediate danger, such as running into traffic, self-injury or aggression requiring urgent behavioral management

red_flags.finding: Suicidal ideation, self-harm or plan to hurt someone
red_flags.meaning: Immediate safety risk; needs urgent mental health evaluation

red_flags.finding: Sudden onset of symptoms in an older adult with no childhood history
red_flags.meaning: Look for another cause such as depression, medication effect, thyroid disease or cognitive impairment

red_flags.finding: Staring spells with loss of awareness
New focal weakness, numbness, gait change or headache
red_flags.meaning: Possible structural neurologic disease; needs urgent imaging
Suggests a primary psychotic disorder rather than ADHD

red_flags.finding: Periods of elevated mood with decreased need for sleep
red_flags.meaning: Suggests bipolar disorder; stimulants can worsen it
Consider abuse or another cause of behavioral change

complications.name: Motor vehicle collisions and driving citations
Relationship conflict and divorce
clues: Partner complaints about forgetfulness or interrupting

complications.name: Injuries from impulsivity
clues: Burns or cuts from careless behavior

special_populations.differences: Diagnosis depends on parent and teacher reports; preschool children present mainly with hyperactivity and tantrums, and behavioral therapy is first-line before medication.
New attention problems in an older adult should prompt evaluation for depression, medication effects, sleep apnea and cognitive impairment rather than assuming ADHD.

Symptoms may become harder to manage with the demands of pregnancy and a new infant; treatment decisions must weigh fetal and breastfeeding safety, and stimulants are usually avoided or used cautiously.
Obesity is more common in people with ADHD and can worsen sleep apnea and daytime attention; weight and sleep should be addressed alongside ADHD treatment.

key_questions.question: When did you or your family first notice these problems?
key_questions.looking_for: Symptoms present since early childhood, before age 12, not a recent change

key_questions.question: Does this happen only at school, or also at home and with friends?
key_questions.looking_for: Symptoms in two or more settings, which is required for the diagnosis

key_questions.question: How long has this been going on?
key_questions.looking_for: At least 6 months of persistent symptoms, not episodic

key_questions.question: Can you tell me about trouble paying attention or finishing tasks?
key_questions.looking_for: Careless mistakes, trouble sustaining attention, not seeming to listen, losing items, forgetting daily activities

key_questions.question: Do you fidget, get up when you are supposed to stay seated, or feel restless inside?
key_questions.looking_for: Hyperactivity, which may be visible in children and internal restlessness in teens and adults

key_questions.question: Do you interrupt people, blurt things out, or have trouble waiting your turn?
How much are these problems affecting school, work, friendships or family life?
key_questions.looking_for: Clear impairment in at least one area, which is required for the diagnosis

key_questions.question: What makes it better or worse?
key_questions.looking_for: Worse with long, boring or quiet tasks; better with breaks, movement, one-on-one attention and structure

key_questions.question: How is sleep? Do you snore or wake up tired?
key_questions.looking_for: Poor sleep or snoring, which can cause or worsen inattention and hyperactivity

key_questions.question: Have you ever had staring spells where you lose awareness and do not remember what happened?
key_questions.looking_for: Absence seizures, which can be mistaken for daydreaming

key_questions.question: Have you had any periods of elevated mood with much less need for sleep?
key_questions.looking_for: Bipolar disorder, which stimulants can worsen

key_questions.question: Any thoughts of hurting yourself or others?
key_questions.looking_for: Immediate safety risk requiring urgent evaluation

key_questions.question: Has anyone in your family had ADHD, learning problems, or repeated grades?
key_questions.looking_for: A strong family history supporting the diagnosis

key_questions.question: How are grades and behavior at school? Any repeated discipline or suspensions?
Do you use any substances, including stimulants, cannabis or alcohol?
key_questions.looking_for: Substance use that could explain the symptoms or complicate treatment

key_questions.question: What medical conditions do you have, and what medications do you take?
key_questions.looking_for: Conditions or medications that can mimic ADHD or affect treatment choice

key_questions.question: Were you born early or with a very low birth weight?
key_questions.looking_for: Prematurity or low birth weight, a known risk factor

key_questions.question: Any problems with vision or hearing?
key_questions.looking_for: Sensory problems that can look like inattention and should be screened

reasoning_points: A persistent pattern of inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity causing impairment
Symptoms present in two or more settings, such as home and school or work
Clear interference with social, academic or occupational functioning
Symptoms not better explained by another condition such as anxiety, depression, a learning disorder, sleep apnea or absence seizures
The presentation type is described by which symptom group predominates over the past 6 months
Information gathered from parents and teachers using standardized rating scales, not the child's self-report alone
Comorbid anxiety, depression, learning disorders, sleep problems and substance use are screened for
Labs and imaging are ordered only to exclude mimics suggested by history or exam, not routinely

easy: School-age boy with classic hyperactivity, fidgeting and interrupting
Symptoms since preschool, present at home and school
Normal exam and normal neurologic exam
medium: Girl with the predominantly inattentive presentation, diagnosed later
Adolescent with declining grades and disorganization but no visible hyperactivity
Symptoms complicated by coexisting anxiety or a learning disorder
Adult presenting with job and relationship problems rather than restlessness
hard: Preschool child presenting mainly with tantrums and hyperactivity
Older adult with new attention problems that turn out to be depression or sleep apnea
Pregnant patient whose symptoms become harder to manage
Patient with staring spells that are actually absence seizures
Symptoms limited to one setting or starting abruptly after a stressor
